text: Eh, couldn’t he have done without him this time, but there you are! Wasn’t it quite enough, after all, for the work to be done only by the official delegates, and yet Bay Ganyo had to stick his nose in too. As if those official ones were not capable of showing the outside world what a Bulgarian and Bulgarian patriotism mean. Why, were such characters as the man with the thick Russian beard, or the one who looks like a little Frenchman and speaks French very briskly and fluently, or, finally, the well-known Bulgarian diplomat, not enough? Indeed, if you ask me, the last one alone was enough for the Russians. The man whom the Russian press calls a Bulgarian diplomat is in fact a soap-maker from Plovdiv. What a progressive nation! When Bulgarian soap-makers pass in Russia for diplomats, just imagine what would happen if a real Bulgarian diplomat were to appear before Mother Russia, eh? However modest you may be, you cannot help being proud! Truly, justice demands that one admit the French are a little like us too: their Félix Faure rose from a leatherworker to become President of the Republic, and the Romans have a similar case as well: do you remember Cincinnatus? But we shall surpass both them and the others. Try, for example, standing in the middle of the bazaar with your eyes blindfolded: I assure you that the first Bulgarian you catch and ask, “Do you wish to become Bulgarian prince?” — without hesitating for a minute, will answer you in the affirmative; perhaps he will only stipulate that the gifts and tips he distributes should be paid not out of his salary, but from the treasury...

The story is about Bay Ganyo... So, that being the case, couldn’t it, I said, have been done without him? Why did he have to represent the Bulgarian people too? But you’ll say that he is not an official delegate. It makes no difference. Once correspondents from important newspapers go to interview him, and his words, like an oracle’s prophecy, are spread through the press all over the world—go and prove afterward that it is not the Bulgarian nation speaking through Bay Ganyo’s mouth...

But I, an incorrigible optimist, think that fate intertwined Bay Ganyo in this mission solely in order to preserve the delegation’s present Bulgarian national character, because, like it or not, a thick Russian beard, a French diplomat — these do not sound Bulgarian. And that Bay Ganyo upheld high and with dignity the banner of Bulgarian patriotism, everyone will clearly see from the following interview. (There is no need to mention that the first gentleman, dressed in a frock coat, who entered Bay Ganyo’s room and before whom Bay Ganyo managed to pour out his brotherly feelings, was not a correspondent, but a waiter from the hotel. A small misunderstanding, but what can you do? With sincere feelings boiling in the chest, eyes clouded by touching tears — it is quite natural for a mistake to happen.)
Enters the correspondent. Whether Bay Ganyo had prepared some chopped onions for himself or not—I do not know, but I can positively affirm that his eyes filled with tears:
— Oh, hello, brother, hello. Nine years, brother, nine! Not a day, not two, nine years — and Bay Ganyo burst into tears.

Anyone would naturally think that the fraternal meeting after a long sorrowful separation would fill Bay Ganyo’s breast with tender feelings and that the overflow of those feelings would flow in the form of touching tears; but what was the correspondent’s astonishment when he saw that instantly his interlocutor’s face cleared up, and heard the following words from his mouth, uttered as if in secret, with a wink:

— But you should know what kind of wreath we’ve made, just say it’s perfect — pure work! Not copper, silver — but pure gold. And do you know how much it costs? What do you think, brother?... If the Russians were to present me, for example, such a wreath, so to speak, I’d kiss their feet — what are you talking about, it’s no joke, gold! And pure gold at that, not just...
— Well, some kind of Macedonian movement has started there in your place — the correspondent diverts the conversation. — Do you find that this movement is timely?

— Movement? What movement?! — Bay Ganyo exclaims, as if hearing of such a thing for the first time. — Come on, don’t worry! There’s no movement at all... A rogue’s business! Bandits! Is this any time for an uprising? And what do those loafers want — I can’t make it out. Your Grace, do you know what? I don’t know whether you know — there is a firman from 1870 for six bishops in Macedonia — they’ve given three, they’ll give three more, and then they’ll all sit down on their backsides! That’s what they’re after!
— What about the Treaty of Berlin?
— Well, shut those up... Let’s talk about something else. Tell me, do you know Dragana Tsankova?
— Yes, I think I know him quite well.
— Well? — and Bay Ganyo emphasized the question with an ambiguous twitch of his fingers. — What do you make of this fellow?
— I think he is a good patriot.

Bay Ganyo laughed unnaturally and shook his head: — Pa-tri-ot? E-he-e, if only you knew what a fellow he is! Has he ever thought for a single day about his fatherland? He only looks to settle himself and his son-in-law. He’s been like that since he was little, I know him. As for patriots, if you ask me, we are real patriots. Just watch me well! For me, not two hundred — one hundred and fifty rubles a month, and you’ll see what your Uncle Ganyo can do... How do you reckon me, your grace! This isn’t Abyssinia...
— Have you had lunch, Mr. Balkanski?
— Why do you ask? Are you inviting me to lunch, or what?... I accept. Aren’t we Slavs?
